title: Maternal responses to infant positive affect and toddler regulation of positive affect: A longitudinal pilot study
abstract: Abstract Children's ability to regulate positive affect (PA) is a crucial yet understudied aspect of early socioemotional development. This pilot study investigated whether maternal responses to infant PA longitudinally predict toddlers’ regulation of PA. Participants were 32 mother–infant dyads from a larger longitudinal study in Toronto, Canada. At 11–12 months, dyads were video recorded during naturalistic play at home. Maternal responses to infant PA were assessed using an observational coding system that distinguishes supportive (e.g., elaborative, matching) from nonsupportive (e.g., intrusive, ignoring) responses. At 18–20 months, toddlers completed the gift delay task, which measures regulation of high‐arousal PA through latency to touch a desirable toy. Multiple regression analysis controlling for age and family income showed that a greater proportion of supportive responses in infancy predicted better regulation of PA in toddlerhood (β = .37, p = .027). Findings provide preliminary evidence that supportive maternal responses to PA in infancy are associated with capacities to regulate PA in toddlerhood. Results highlight the importance of examining positive as well as negative affect in models of early emotion regulation and suggest potential targets for early intervention.
